text: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string among an array of strings. If there's no common prefix, return an empty string.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the common prefix has to be shared by every string, from the start of each. Can the array contain an empty string, and is it guaranteed non-empty?
At least one string, each up to two hundred characters, lowercase. An individual string could be empty.
Let me run through examples. Flower, flow, flight gives f-l. Dog, racecar, car gives the empty string — nothing shared. And if any string is empty, the answer must be the empty string.

Let me think. The common prefix must be a prefix of every string, so in particular a prefix of the first one. This problem reminds me of horizontal scanning: start with the first string as the candidate prefix, then for each string, shrink the prefix from the right until it's actually a prefix of that string. Since each string only tightens the constraint, the prefix only ever gets shorter, so it converges, and I can bail out early once it's empty.
How do you test whether prefix is a prefix of str?

Str dot find of prefix equals zero. Find returns the first position where prefix occurs; position zero means it starts at the very beginning — that is, it's a prefix. Anything else — a positive position, or n-pos for not found — means it isn't, so I chop the last character and retry. Nicely, when prefix shrinks to empty, finding the empty string returns zero, so the loop stops cleanly without an underflow.

Here's the plan. One: set prefix to the first string. Two: for each string, while prefix doesn't sit at position zero, drop its last character. Three: if prefix ever becomes empty, return the empty string right away; otherwise return prefix at the end. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Here's the code. One loop over the strings, and inside it a while loop that trims the prefix until it matches the start of the current string, plus an early return once it's empty. One thing worth flagging — the loop compares find's result with zero, not with n-pos. A not-found check would accept a prefix that appears in the middle of the string, which is wrong. This runs in big O of S, where S is the total number of characters. Extra space is just the prefix.
Is there a faster approach, and does yours handle the empty-string case?

The empty case is handled for free: if any string is empty, prefix gets chopped all the way to empty and I return early — no special-casing. For speed, a vertical scan is often better: compare column zero of all strings, then column one, and stop at the first mismatch or when any string ends. Its edge is early termination — if the prefix is short, it stops after a few columns instead of scanning a long string with find. Both are big O of S worst case; vertical wins when the common prefix is short relative to the strings, horizontal wins on brevity of code.

Let's dry-run flower, flow, flight — expected f-l. Flower leaves the prefix as flower, and flow trims it to flow. The row that matters is flight: flow doesn't start flight, so I chop to f-l-o, still no match, then to f-l, which sits at position zero. So it returns f-l. That matches. Also checked: dog, racecar, car chops to empty on the second string; a single string returns itself; and an empty string next to a-b-c gives the empty string. I verified against a character-by-character reference on five thousand random inputs — zero mismatches.

Time is big O of S, space is constant beyond the prefix. Oh, one more thing — if I had to answer many prefix queries or group strings by shared prefix, I'd build a trie instead; the common prefix is just the path from the root until it branches. And a neat property: the longest common prefix is associative, so for huge inputs you can divide and conquer or parallelize the merge. The same trick handles the longest common suffix: reverse every string, run this, reverse the result.
Nice. You anchored on prefix of the first string, used find equals zero cleanly, knew why the empty case falls out for free, and offered the vertical scan and trie as alternatives. Solid.
